## M0-E01

**Peek at the first five books** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture2 L42-48](../sources/lecture2.txt) *“but limit now to the first five rows”*

```sql
SELECT "title", "year" FROM "books" ORDER BY "id" LIMIT 5;
```

**Why:** `LIMIT` caps the rows. Without `ORDER BY`, "the first five" is whatever order SQLite happens to read the table in.
That is usually rowid order, but it is not guaranteed, so we make it explicit.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title | year |
|---|---|
| Boulder | 2023 |
| Whale | 2023 |
| The Gospel According to the New World | 2023 |
| Standing Heavy | 2023 |
| Time Shelter | 2023 |

</details>

## M0-E02

**Search for a movie by title** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L116-123](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Came out in 2006 and the ID is 317219.”*

## M0-E05

**Tally raw votes** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L1229-1246](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“Why do I have so many?”*

```sql
SELECT "title", COUNT("title") FROM "votes" GROUP BY "title";
```

**Why:** GROUP BY compares text exactly. `'Farmers Working at Dawn'` and `'farmers working at dawn'` and `' Spring outing'` (leading space) are all different groups.
Fixing this is exercise M2-E13.

## M0-E06

**Average rating per book** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L423-433](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“I should see I have rounded ratings now”*, [lecture4 L374-386](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“3.67 book 1 and 2.5 for book 2”*

```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating"
FROM "ratings"
GROUP BY "book_id";
```

**Why:** Book 1 has ratings 4, 3, 4, so its average is 3.67. Book 2 has 2 and 3, so 2.5. These are the two values on the lecture's slide.

## M0-E08

**Fernanda Melchor's books, with nested subqueries** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L168-192](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“then find the titles associated with those book IDs themselves”*, [lecture4 L296-297](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“Fernanda has written Paradais and Hurricane Season”*

```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "books"
WHERE "id" IN (
    SELECT "book_id" FROM "authored"
    WHERE "author_id" = (
        SELECT "id" FROM "authors"
        WHERE "name" = 'Fernanda Melchor'
    )
);
```

**Why:** Three tables are needed because books and authors are linked through the junction table `authored`.
Lecture 4 then shows how a view collapses this to one line (M3-E02).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title |
|---|
| Paradais |
| Hurricane Season |

</details>

## M0-E09

**Author names next to book titles, with JOIN** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture4 L203-240](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“JOIN books ON books dot id equals, in this case, authored dot book_id”*

```sql
SELECT "name", "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id";
```

**Why:** This is the query behind the `longlist` view in Lecture 4. Each JOIN lines up a primary key with the matching foreign key ("touching your fingertips together", L68).

## D0-01

**The NULL that never matches** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture3 L734-741](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“WHERE "acquired" IS NOT NULL”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "collections" WHERE "acquired" = NULL;
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "collections" WHERE "acquired" IS NULL;
```

**Diagnosis (null):** `= NULL` is never true. NULL means unknown, so use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title |
|---|
| Imaginative Landscape |

</details>

## D0-02

**Joined on the wrong column** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture4 L207-219](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“linking it up by looking at the authors dot ID column”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
WHERE "name" = 'Fernanda Melchor';
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "authors"
JOIN "authored" ON "authors"."id" = "authored"."author_id"
JOIN "books" ON "books"."id" = "authored"."book_id"
WHERE "name" = 'Fernanda Melchor';
```

**Diagnosis (join):** The broken query matched author id 24 with **book** id 24, which is a coincidence of numbers, not a relationship.
Ids from different tables share values (lecture2 L310-326), so the database can't catch this. Only you can.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title |
|---|
| Paradais |
| Hurricane Season |

</details>

## D0-03

**Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture4 L344-351](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“books had individual ratings from individual people”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "books"
JOIN "ratings" ON "ratings"."book_id" = "books"."id"
WHERE "year" = 2022;
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "books"
WHERE "year" = 2022
AND "id" IN (SELECT "book_id" FROM "ratings");
```

**Diagnosis (duplicates):** Joining to the "many" side of a one-to-many relationship multiplies rows.

## D0-04

**One average instead of one per book** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture4 L403-407](../sources/lecture4.txt) *“That means I'll calculate the average rating for each book ID.”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating" FROM "ratings";
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "book_id", ROUND(AVG("rating"), 2) AS "rating" FROM "ratings" GROUP BY "book_id";
```

**Diagnosis (aggregation):** SQLite even let you select the bare `book_id` next to the aggregate (it picks an arbitrary row's value). Most other DBMSs reject that query outright.

## D0-05

**`=` with a subquery that returns many rows** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture5 L376-379](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“I'll say WHERE the "id" of that movie is IN some list of movie IDs”*

Broken version:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" = (
    SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (
        SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'
    )
);
```

Fixed:
```sql
SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" IN (
    SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (
        SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'
    )
);
```

**Diagnosis (subquery):** Use `IN` when a subquery can return several rows. `=` is fine for the innermost one, since there is one Tom Hanks.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

| title |
|---|
| Forrest Gump |
| Apollo 13 |
| Toy Story |
| Toy Story 2 |
| Saving Private Ryan |
| Cast Away |
| Toy Story 3 |
| Toy Story 4 |

</details>
